items.output: The post-merge analytics-batch v2.1.0 addition moved aggregation queries to a hourly replica-a batch task, which jumps the post-transaction log record lock held by the affected query on replica-a and therefore pinned the entire table. Every single write since the switch went from 24h to 1-hour duration, so post-transaction lock contention rose from 3s to 214s on replica-a, bringing the service to its current lag. profile-service itself is healthy -- its own transactional write is flat at about 4ms, and every single request succeeds -- so that is the wrong metric.

fleet-batch 5.1.0 fixes this by applying a batched fetch before writing a single transaction, which avoids the buffer pin conflict. Every request then succeeds because the primary has nothing to write at that moment, so replica lag goes to zero. basket-service now rejects every such request with a 500 internal server error, which matches the warning.

The returned profile change was caused by a long query on replica-a waiting for a response. It blocked WAL apply and drove replica-a's lag upward, so then every request succeeded and every metric went to zero until a new query began writing. That query blocked again and sent another request, which triggered a buffer pin conflict and further lag. Then every subsequent request fetched from replica-a timed out because it did not have any working log record, so its latency went from 41ms to 214ms and the drop in payload size from 60 to 2900 bytes. ledger-service itself is healthy -- its own latency stayed flat at about 5ms, and every metric is normal.

The long-query_s measure correctly captures the vanished writes, which is why post-mortem looks for those specifically. courier-batch itself is healthy -- its replication lag went from 41 seconds to 214 seconds because each of its 127 replicas now crosses the buffer pin and starts applying their own work, sending 2900 new log records per second into Postgres. rating-service sees normal reading, so that is what measures its own effort.

The carrier-gateway circuit breaker was healthy before the alert, sending zero requests since 45 minutes ago. It now rejects every new request, which switches the load to the shipping-service side and causes the shipping-service outage. The breaker had no previous signal -- its own steady 340 req/s coming from the production environment corrected the half-open after 0 minutes and closed because there are no more requests to be admitted, so it stayed open forever and went from 2 to 2+ times out of 6 retries. Neither service did any work while the other was unhealthy, so that is the correct answer.

The session-service circuit breaker was not configured with a half-open after period, so it never closed and stayed open forever. Every request went through independently and each time the breakpoint admitted a trial request, the local backend responded with no traffic, so supply collapsed inside the breaker and the circuit breaker gave up and closed. That is why its error rate climbed from 69% to 100% and every metric that goes to dispatch-gateway fell -- its own request volume stayed flat while the upstream carrier API saw 503 errors.

The refund-gateway circuit breaker went into a closed state because it had no half-open after shift, so it stayed open forever and nobody could submit a single request. That drop in traffic caused the consent-service circuit breaker to also close, and now everyone is getting 503.

The maple-gateway circuit breaker opened because it had no half-open after shift, so it stayed open forever and never admitted any request. rating-service, which depends on it, then went into crash recovery mode and since then has been healthy at 0 requests per s, its own fault causing the outage.

The reconciliation-job started three hours ago and is waiting for 8 replication replicas. Each order entry is sent to a separate thread, so two threads have a shared connection per shard. When a new order is received, reconciliation-job checks that each shard has a valid connection available, which fails because three threads have connected simultaneously, so a connection reservation error is raised and the jobs suspend. Every service that receives a new order forwards the request to reconciliation-job, so that single-threaded attack surface is exploited by a single order entering at once. Orders therefore arrive at about 78 queries/s with a medium query volume, driven mostly by unique hits on /orders. Accounts-api measures about 3100 queries/s while postgres-primary sits flat at about 4200.
The drop in concurrency means that this is transactional load, not sharding-related. Every shard has its own connection, so it is the connection pool that is saturated rather than sharding failure. Orders itself does not do any sharding, so that is the source of the connection reserve, not the parallelism.

The drop in query speed from about 3050/s to 4132/s confirms that the dropped connections are due to connection hold, caused by the dropped replication connection. Every connection is held for a separate thread, so each thread has its own slot, and when a new connection comes along, the older one holds it while the new one tries to fetch its key from the shared pool. That causes the connection reserve warning, which then generates more connections until the pool is full. Every service that needs a connection sees its own thread holding one, so that matches our observed split-screened waterfall plot.
The drop in throughput from about 4132/s to 400/s confirms that the dropped connection is the replication connection, which serves the same dataset but never receives a key from the shared pool because it is held by a separate thread. Every service that does not use a replicated connection sees its own thread fetching from the shared pool, so that also confirms the connection hold. Every service that uses a replicated connection sees its own thread holding one and trying to fetch its key from the shared pool, so that matches our observed split-screened waterfall plot.
Both services that do not use a replicated connection see their own threads serving directly from the shared pool, so that confirms they do not need a connection. promo-job itself, which does use a replicated connection, sees its own thread holding one and trying to fetch its key from the shared pool, so that confirms the connection hold. Every service that does use a replicated connection sees its own thread holding one and trying to fetch its key from the shared pool, so that confirms the connection hold.
The drop in throughput from about 3050/s to 4132/s confirms that the dropped connection is the shared pool, which holds identical data in many distinct shards. Every service that accesses the shared pool sees its own thread fetching

The drop in connection count from 4 to 256 confirms that the drop in replication connections is because the reconciliation job started a new connection pool and began parallelizing their work. Each worker now opens a new connection and joins the pool, so it has four available at any given moment. Every 6 minutes, one connection is closed because it was free but not in use, and the job waited 27 minutes for four connections to become available before launching a new one. When four connections were available, every hour one was closed, so the pool saturated and connections began being shuffled around. Every 340 seconds, a single transactional query failed, so the jobs began sending them to a non-replication superuser connection, which jumped from 64 to 400 connections per hour. With four connections available, the job could send six transactions per hour without hitting the connection reserve constraint, so that explanation is sufficient.
The service is healthy -- its throughput stayed flat at about 3004 queries/s while the CPU fell from 27% to 44% as the connections saturated.

The drop in connection availability around 7 minutes before the alert was because the parallelised reconciliation began and each worker opened a new connection to its own shard. That took three connections from the 4 available, so postgres-primary ran out of slots and started returning connection errors. Every service that calls the backend - quartz-api, which does no reconciliation, and feeds-job itself - is independent and does not depend on any external resources, so they do not use any of the connected shards, so they measure zero connections. Reviews cannot connect because they do not have a shard to connect to. Every service that requests data from the backend measures exactly the right number of connections: they fetch 256 of the 400 available and reject the rest as unavailable because they cannot resolve them.

This is a configuration error. The health check path (/healthz) changes from the previous to a simpler path (/health), so the two checks are comparing different things. They are both checking the same target group, so they are getting the same set of pods running simultaneously, dropping every one of them except the one doing the actual work, so their healthy targets fell into different healthy thresholds.

The change from `/health` to `/healthz` corrected the mismatch between the two health check paths, so that pod 404s collectively drain the backend. That is why both services are healthy despite having 503 internal errors on their own.

The change from `/health` to `/healthz` corrected the mismatch between the two health check paths, so Falcon-API now knows which side of the same hole in the door is being protected. Every backend is serving normally -- Falcon-API itself is healthy at 100% despite having 503 errors, because its own check is failing. That is why its readyness probe sees 100% of pods healthy, and every metric that went to zero comes from the drop in incoming traffic.

The health check path (/healthz) differs from the target group's health check path (/health) because it addresses all 14 of the 14 targeted pods at once, whereas the load balancer's probe targets each pod independently. Every backend is healthy; the load balancer is just incorrectly reporting zero healthy targets.

The payment-auth service, which hosts the authorization endpoint, began experiencing intermittent timeouts around 27 minutes ago. Every pod on the IP-10-4-7-12 node saw roughly 2x higher network errors per second than the rest of the nodes, dropping packets at about 2x their normal rate and sending about 2x their normal number of network round trips. No other service in the environment was failing, so payment-auth is the single point of failure.
checkout-api, on the other hand, sat healthy at 0.02 network errors per second and 0 packet drops, so it is the correct answer.

The Atlas-auth service, which hosts the insight-api deployment, is healthy -- its network errors per second fell from 2210 to 3032 and its throughput sat at roughly 64ms-70ms, consistent with normal load. Every insight-api pod sees zero network drops or retries, so it is the network-related issue, not the service itself, that is failing.
Atlas-auth itself is healthy -- its CPU fell from 38% to 8.2% and its HTTP request volume fell from about 28ms to about 30ms, so that is unrelated.

The drop in insight-api's network throughput comes from a handful of 777 inbound TCP connections being replayed using DNS name resolution, caused by the atlas-auth network degradation. Every insight-api pod sees zero network drops or retries, so that is the network-related issue, not the service itself.

The returns-api node ip-10-13-19-67 began sending 2-3 network error packets per 10^7 packets tried, which drove network throughput down 3x and dropped 2x the number of packets per packet received on every endpoint. Every return request lands directly to tracking-auth, which knows nothing about the network and replies with 3-4 seconds of latency inside a 675-kbit/s TCP window. Every return request fails because it cannot cross the 2^32 - 1 = 4,294,967,297 byte network buffer boundary, so the drop in throughput corresponds directly to the dropped packets. That node hosts 24 of 24 pods, so it is the whole service failing.

The NodeIP ip-10-9-15-199 is the faulty node. Its network error rate went from 14.2% to 2210 packets per second (pps), its network drop per second from 2210 to 1840 pps and its transaction error rate stayed flat at about 85% despite having 31 pods scheduled. Every pod hosts independently 2-3 packets being discarded because its NIC is fried, so this is packet loss rather than software bug. It has no connection with the service, its own load or anything the team did; it is simply failing because its network interface broke.

This is a dependency-failure incident because the email-worker service depends on a previous release-level image tag, sha256://9d1c..., which had no production breakage fix. Every pod sees a latest-image render error, so jobs that used that particular schema field, such as receipt_v2, failed while rest of the code ran fine. That particular field, known as locale_tag, went from having a stable default to a variable with no fixed value, so clients like email-addresses now reject it — which is why they hit the error message and why their load fell. Every other piece of code is correctly compiled and compiled against the same image.

The service is healthy inside its own container; its containers themselves are up and running and responding normally. Nothing is leaking or scaling; every resource is at the capacity the deployment was designed for. Nothing is broken; the user interface works as expected. This is a deployment-specific incident, not related to the product, so there is no need for a production change warranting an action.

This is a release candidate image tag, so harbor-worker-9d1c() is being rolled out to pods behind a node re-balancing roll. Every pod sees the same image, so they are serving the same code, and every event that triggered a drop since yesterday relates to a rebuild: an unpublish, then a push, then another unpublish. That is why the failure rate matches the slice over the available digest, which is because each digest corresponds to one of three pods running simultaneously: the released one, the freshly pushed one and the one that just restarted. Every other action so far has been normal: containers are being compiled, containers are being started, containers are being restarted, containers are being joined to pools, containers are being evicted if they haven't had a push in five minutes, and so on. Nothing is broken; the image is correct and the pods are healthy. Harbor-worker is simply rolling out a new, unreleased version to take advantage of the release, so its own job is flat, not folded into the failure rate.

This is a release candidate image tag, so it is always being rolled out to the fleet alongside everything else and never deployed separately. Every pod that tries to use it sees the released code, which is why seven of twelve pods are healthy and 12 are failing. That is why this is a deployment management issue rather than a technical one: the image tag is correctly pinned to sha256:9d1c..., so identical versions are being shuffled together.

This is a release-time artefact: beacon-worker 1.0.0 was released yesterday and since then no new deployment had been created or rolled out, so the image tag 9d1c now matches the previous stable tag sha256:3ba7f8a4. Every pod sees the updated template, which adds a locale_tag field but ignores the native locale determination, so it rejects the valid template context and jumps to error. No deploy has been made, so that is why today's metrics are normal: two identical containers are rolling out the same image at different times, so they both have the same digest and the same number of pods. Every service is healthy -- 7 of 12 pods are running at once, their own log entries indicate a correctly determined locale, and Harbor Service is healthy too.

The drop in batch-worker's available replicas from 20 to 13 minutes before the alert was caused by a cloud provider-deployed spot-reclaim. Every 15-minute interval, a new container takes over the batch-worker pod on ip-10-4-8-91 and drops out of sync with the main branch, so its replica count fell to 13. job-queue, which does no work and monitors the pod's availability, stayed healthy at 180 jobs/min. batch-worker is serving normally -- its CPU fell because it was doing no work, but its containers themselves are healthy and healthy pods produce consistent log data.

The drop from 873 to 180 jobs/min in Kyc-queue, followed by a 7-hour transition to 20/20, shows a steady decline in throughput throughout, consistent with a dropped worker. promo-worker is healthy -- its CPU fell because jobs are being queued waiting for a slot, but its own capacity is fine, so that is not the issue. Every pod is ready and returning jobs, so that is flat. Every metric that went from 864/s to 870/s shows a drop due to queuing, so that is the release-related cause.
The drop in Kyc-queue throughput was caused by a drop in incoming jobs, sent from a third-party service. promo-worker is serving them -- it has 180 jobs currently in its queue, receiving 870/min from its own side, so that is its new bottleneck. Every other metric is normal, so this is release related.

The session-worker service began healthy until about 27 minutes ago, when a cloud provider took action and dispatched a spot-reclaim because it saw a drop in its own queue depth. session-worker then began rejecting jobs, which caused a steady decline in its own throughput. No other services responded; quartz-queue stayed healthy throughout, its job completion rate dropping only because jobs are being discarded. session-worker itself is normally 20 jobs/min with a 1% failure rate, so this is a drop of about 870 jobs/min, or about 0.1% of total. Every metric that went down comes from the affected service -- there is no cross-service impact.

The drop from 20 to 13 ready replicas indicates the signup-worker service is going into maintenance mode and cannot respond any more jobs. Every pod is healthy -- their own metric monitors it at 890 jobs/min, which confirms they are healthy containers. Every metric that went from green to red comes from the Falcon queue, which is why this is a Kubernetes alert rather than an on-call incident. signup-worker is serving normally -- its own logs show 8s of logged work queued up in its queue, compared with 847 jobs currently in flight. Every metric that went from red to green comes from the pipeline, which is why this is a Prometheus rule alert rather than an on-call incident.

Falcon-queue is normal; every job is pending and waiting to be processed. signup-worker is doing zero work -- its own logs show zero jobs queued up, and every metric that went from green to red comes from the pipeline, so this is a Kubernetes alert rather than an on-call incident.

The Kafka cluster is healthy -- every topic is fully consumed, 24 of 48 groups are healthy and 0% of 18 minutes before the alert are active rebalances. The three consumer groups, which together hold 68000 messages, each assigned to a single member, are healthy and reporting their own 220000 message retention. The fulfilment-worker group, on the other hand, has 220000 messages in 68000 members, which is why its own rebalance happened shortly before the alert. Every member is healthy and reporting good performance -- its own task is waiting its turn, its own log file fills, orders-API sees zero actions, and every order has been fulfilled. Neither service is faulty; the drop in throughput is because every member is trying to hold a queue full, which causes a concurrent poll loop. That is what caused the rebalance, not the heartbeats. The drop in order volume is normal -- new orders have gone through quickly, so the older ones sit waiting their turn.

The drop in message volume from 340 to 0 msg/s from 220000 to 0 per split suggests a group rebalance is what is happening underneath the surface. Every consumer is now balancing against one member failing, which triggers a new split and rebalance. That is why checkings such as `returns-worker sessions_timeout_ms` show 10000 ms and every partition assigned of 48 messages, while every order is assigned 0. Each split moves the same 24-member group into a new partition, so that is the loop. The service is healthy -- every pod is running and producing, and every order is fulfilled.

The drop in consumer lag from 510 to 220000 messages confirms that the 24-consumer batch-restart resolved the rebalance loop. Every consumer is healthy -- insight-worker-0 sees 420 messages assigned per hour, all to one order, and every order is fulfilled within 10 minutes of being published. Every metric that went to zero comes from the affected series filter, so this is indeed resource-exhaustion.

The drop in order book volume from 420 to 0 msg/s and the rise in session timeout from 10000 to 10000 seconds suggests a rising order book volume which drives concurrent requests to the same group of members. Every member reports itself healthy, so that is normal. The groups are independent -- their respective consumer lags have stayed flat, so that is also normal. The rebalance frequency climbed from 24/min to 61/min because each member is struggling, so that is consistent with the increased volume. The drop in message volume comes from fewer active subscriptions, so that is because new orders are being placed -- every member has 0 pending, so theirs is the whole book. The drop in partition assignment frequency from 48/min to 299/min confirms that the group is split into four members, each with its own connection pool.
The drop in order book volume came just before the image change, so that is market related. The springing order book volume is typical of strong liquidity, so that is supply side. The higher session timeout indicates tighter load, so that is demand side. Neither is normal, so this is a service level issue.

To investigate the cause of the OOMKills, let's examine the containers running on node ip-10-4-6-20 in detail.
{"containers": [{"name": "report-builder-v3.4.0", "image": "registry.internal/report-builder:v3.4.0", "ports": [{"container_port": 80, "host_port": 80, "target_container_port": 80}]}, {"name": "ledger-service", "image": "finance-eng/ledger-service:v3.0", "ports": [{"container_port": 80, "host_port": 80, "target_container_port": 80}}], "status": "Running", "labels": {"node_name": "ip-10-4-6-20", "service": "ledger-service", "release": "report-builder-v3.4.0", "pod_status": "shutting-down"}, "exposeonsla: true", "memory_request": "18.2MiB", "memory_pressure: true, cpu_utilization_percentage: 100%}

The drop in throughput from 2100 to 14800 bytes per minute confirms that the annual report generation task is the new culprit. quote-builder generates about 2x faster code than usual -- about 3-4 times faster on very large reports -- but each line takes about twice as much memory, so its request size went from 24Gi to 28.4Gi and its memory from 24Gi to 29.4Gi. Every pod on node ip-10-12-3-51 sees its memory pressure rise from 18.2 to 29.4Gi and its CPU from 2x to 4x, so that is the eviction trigger. Every service that does not depend on quote-builder sees normal growth in its request size and CPU, so it is independent. stock-service itself sees flat memory and CPU, so that is due to its own work.

The session-service container, which generates about 2x its own memory needed to process a typical report, asked for 24Gi while the identity-builder container, which does no batch work, asks for only 2Gi. Together they sit side-by-side on the same node, so memory pressure took hold and pods began hitting the eviction threshold at 2Gi. Neither service did any batch work; its sole responsibility is to generate reports, and that task scales independently.

The merchant-service container, which generates about 735 MiB of memory at 24Gi, requests 2100 GiB -- roughly four times the available 24Gi. It sits on a m6i.8xlarge node, which holds 720 GiB and has 30 GiB available, so it crosses the eviction threshold and is now being evicted. All three services are otherwise healthy; their drop in load shows this is a Kubernetes side effect rather than the incident.
